chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from Ali ibn Uqba from Burayd ibn Mu'awiya from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'A man made a bequest to me, and I asked him to include a relative of his with me, so he did. And I mentioned that the one who made the bequest said that the one I included in the bequest owed him five hundred dirhams, with a silver bowl as a pledge for it. When the man died, the executor began to claim that he owed him several measures of wheat.' He said, 'If he produces evidence, [he gets it]; otherwise, he has nothing.'

I said to him, 'Is it permissible for him to take something from what is in his hand?' He said, 'It is not permissible for him.' I said, 'What do you think if a man attacked him and took his property, and was able to take from his property what he took? Would that be permissible for him?' He said, 'Indeed, this is not like that.'
ai.seo_question: Can an executor deduct a deceased person's debts from the heir's share without proof?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the distinction between a creditor's right to claim a debt from an estate and the executor's authority to deduct it unilaterally. He establishes that while the heir is not obligated to pay the debt from their share without proof, the creditor cannot simply seize assets by force, as 'taking by claim' differs fundamentally from 'taking by ownership.' This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that debt settlement requires verified evidence or mutual agreement, protecting the heir's inherited rights from arbitrary deduction.
